reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic Python example: a = [[1], [2]]; b = a.copy(). The outer lists are distinct, but their corresponding inner lists are shared references.
After b[0].append(9), both a and b display [[1, 9], [2]]. The inner object changed; no outer slot was replaced.
After b.append([3]), a remains [[1, 9], [2]], while b becomes [[1, 9], [2], [3]]. This append changes only the copied outer list.
A tuple can also contain a mutable list: t = ([1],); t[0].append(2) succeeds and t becomes ([1, 2],). Reassigning t[0] raises TypeError because the tuple slot is immutable.
Mutability describes operations on a particular object, not automatic immutability of everything reachable from it. A shallow copy is not recursive isolation.

reasoningSteps: Use synthetic Python sets a = {1, 2, 2, 3} and b = {3, 4}. Repeating an equal element does not create an additional member, so len(a) is 3.
Their union has members 1, 2, 3 and 4; their intersection is {3}; a - b is {1, 2}; and their symmetric difference has members 1, 2 and 4.
Set iteration order is not a sorting contract. Use sorted(a | b) when a deterministic ascending presentation of these integers is required.
A set cannot contain a mutable list: { [1] } raises TypeError because the list is unhashable. A frozenset of hashable elements can itself be a member of a set.
Do not infer that every immutable-looking object is hashable: a tuple containing a list is also unhashable. Membership uses hashing and equality rules, not merely the printed form.

software-v06-python-exceptions.verifiedBoundary: Python exceptions signal errors or other exceptional conditions and propagate until handled by a matching exception handler or terminate the current execution context.
software-v06-python-exceptions.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a recipe being carried out in a kitchen with ingredients, tools, tests, and feedback. Software mechanisms are more precise than the analogy; use it only as a memory scaffold.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic Python try block that raises ValueError. Put except Exception before except ValueError in the same try statement.
ValueError is an Exception subclass, so the first broad matching handler runs. The later ValueError handler is not reached for that exception.
Reversing the handlers lets the specific ValueError handler run. Handler ordering therefore matters when exception classes overlap by inheritance.
If the try suite completes normally, an else clause runs; if a handler handles the raised exception, that else clause does not run. A finally clause runs on ordinary exits from either path.

These control-flow rules do not justify catching every error indiscriminately. Unexpected exceptions should retain useful evidence or propagate according to the caller contract; process termination is outside the ordinary cleanup guarantee.

When __exit__ returns False, exit is logged and ValueError propagates to an outer handler. The ordinary trace is enter, body, exit, caught.
When __exit__ returns True, the exception is suppressed and execution continues after the with statement. The trace is enter, body, exit, after.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic Python sequence values = [10, 20, 30] and it = iter(values). The iterator stores traversal state separate from the list object.
Calling next(it) returns 10. Calling list(it) afterward returns [20, 30], consuming only the remaining values.
A second list(it) returns [], and next(it, 'done') returns 'done'. Without a default, next(it) raises StopIteration after exhaustion.
Creating iter(values) again produces a fresh iterator, so list(iter(values)) returns [10, 20, 30]. iter(it) returns the existing iterator rather than restarting it.

An iterable is not necessarily a reusable iterator. Exhaustion remains exhausted under the iterator protocol; this exercise does not rely on behavior when the underlying list is mutated during traversal.

reasoningSteps: A function decorated with contextlib.contextmanager must yield exactly one value. Its first part performs entry, the with body runs at the yield boundary, and the generator resumes for exit.
An exception from the with body is raised inside the generator at its suspended yield. Catching that exception and returning normally tells the manager it was handled.
In a logger that catches ValueError, append 'caught' and use bare raise when the intention is only observation. The same ValueError then propagates, while finally still appends 'cleanup'.
Omitting that raise suppresses the body ValueError; execution continues after the with statement. Logging and suppression are distinct policies.
A generator that yields no value fails before the body; one that yields a second value fails on normal exit. Both are RuntimeError protocol violations, not a way to offer multiple body executions.

reasoningSteps: Use a generator that appends 'start', yields 1, and has a finally clause appending 'cleanup'. Creating the generator does not yet execute its body.
After next(g), the events are ['start']. Calling g.close() raises GeneratorExit at the suspended yield and executes the finally clause, producing ['start','cleanup'].
Calling close again does not run cleanup twice, and next on the closed generator raises StopIteration. This fixture does not return a value from its finally clause.
A for loop break does not itself call close on an arbitrary generator. Keep a reference to g, break after its first item, and observe no cleanup until explicit close.
Do not rely on garbage-collection timing as a portable cleanup policy. This lesson tests synchronous generators and explicit close, not asynchronous generator cancellation or process-crash recovery.
Reference: https://docs.python.org/3.13/reference/expressions.html . These examples concern synchronous Python control flow with inert local objects.

Python dictionaries map hashable keys to values and preserve insertion order as part of the language behavior in current Python versions.
Python sets are unordered collections of distinct hashable objects and support mathematical set-style operations such as union and intersection.
Python exceptions signal errors or other exceptional conditions and propagate until handled by a matching exception handler or terminate the current execution context.
Python context managers define setup and cleanup behavior used by the with statement, commonly to guarantee resource-release logic.
Python iterators implement an iteration protocol that produces successive values until StopIteration signals exhaustion.

vocabulary.definition: Python built-in types differ in mutability: for example, lists are mutable sequences while tuples are immutable sequences.
Python dictionaries map hashable keys to values and preserve insertion order as part of the language behavior in current Python versions.
Python sets are unordered collections of distinct hashable objects and support mathematical set-style operations such as union and intersection.
Python exceptions signal errors or other exceptional conditions and propagate until handled by a matching exception handler or terminate the current execution context.
Python context managers define setup and cleanup behavior used by the with statement, commonly to guarantee resource-release logic.
Python iterators implement an iteration protocol that produces successive values until StopIteration signals exhaustion.
